title: No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion
description: Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom
body: Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom of movement.Asked earlier by broadcasters if he could introduce freedom of movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no".But sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made and the prime minister's deputy spokesperson later said the government was not going to "get ahead" of how to consult the public.Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options.He told broadcasters that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.And he has previously stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.After lengthy questioning about the issue, Number 10 sought to clarify the prime minister's remarks, saying: "The prime minister isn't proposing a return to freedom of movement or any option.""He is crucially not leaning either way and that will be for the British public to decide," the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said."What he wants to do first is have a conversation with the public. The process will follow."She added: "The PM thinks the Brexit deal is not good enough."Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.In an interview with the Sunday Times, external, Burnham said he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and the EU.The PM argued that the type of migration had changed since Brexit, with more foreigners moving permanently.In contrast, he suggested that when the UK was a member of the EU, migration was "generally younger people", who would spend a few years in the country before returning home.However, Burnham added: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."The Schengen Agreement, which the UK was not part of when it was in the EU, allows passport-free travel across member countries. The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.Burnham has argued that since Brexit, the UK has lost immigration control the country previously had."For instance, the small boats crisis has arisen in the last 10 years because we lost that returns agreement when people came here that we could work with other countries to return them," he told broadcasters.The Conservatives and Reform UK both oppose a return to free movement with the EU.However, the Liberal Democrats have argued that allowing freedom of movement would help economic growth.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued most people who voted for Brexit did so because they did not want free movement, while Reform leader Nigel Farage has said such a move would be "a total betrayal of Brexit Britain".Farage told broadcasters he was "up for the fight again" on the EU and an "election is coming" to decide that."Crucially, [Burnham] goes to Brussels on 20 November for a key summit - he must not sign up to anything there without at least putting those minor changes to a general election," he said.

schema.headline: No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion

title: Ethiopia attacks: More than 60 Orthodox Christians killed in Oromia
description: More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks on Christians in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the country's Orthodox Church.One
body: More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks on Christians in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the country's Orthodox Church.One resident, whose 75-year-old father was killed, described it as an ambush. "We were completely unprepared and had no prior knowledge. They surrounded us from all four directions," he told BBC Amharic.The regional government said that it would take action against those responsible.A local official blamed the attacks on a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). The OLA has not commented but has denied carrying out previous such attacks.A statement from the Holy Synod of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church said that 20 houses were burnt to the ground in the attacks. It did not say who was responsible.Eyewitness told BBC Amharic that five of those killed were children.A church official described the attacks on three areas in the Shirka district as a "massacre", saying security forces arrived at the scene but were unable to stop the assault.Many residents have now fled the area.Condemning the violence, the Orthodox Church said attacks against Christians had been increasing recently, and that "such actions undermine the country's values of mutual respect and peaceful coexistence".In a statement posted on Facebook, the Orthodox Church said it had repeatedly raised concerns about insecurity with authorities at different levels of government, but that "so far there has been no solution".The Ethiopian Human Rights Council, a non-governmental organisation, said in a report released in July 2026 that 458 people had been killed in attacks in that area over the previous four years.But this is one of the most deadly attacks in that period.The report said armed groups had repeatedly targeted local communities, particularly followers of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, in what it described as religiously motivated attacks.The government has previously blamed the OLA for the attacks, with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed saying violence targeting civilians and religious institutions was part of a plan to destabilise the country.The group, which says it is fighting for greater rights for the Oromo people, denies these allegations.Previous reports have also documented attacks against Muslims in the area. Residents who spoke to the BBC on various occasions have described the violence as both ethnic and religious in nature.About two-thirds of Ethiopians are Christians, mostly Orthodox, while one third are Muslim.

schema.headline: Ethiopia attacks: More than 60 Orthodox Christians killed in Oromia

title: Brazil election: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic comeback over Bolsonaro
description: Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.Le
body: Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since Brazil's return to civilian rule in 1985 to be elected after losing the first round of voting.Lula told jubilant crowds his victory was a "loss for negativity, lies", adding "long live democracy".Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled. World leaders have congratulated Lula on his re-election.Bolsonaro's rejection comes as no surprise to observers. His father did the same. But a challenge appears unlikely to succeed.Firstly, it seems to centre on the unprecedented decision by the Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting nationwide by two hours. Some Bolsonaro fans are pointing out that Zanin was once Lula's lawyer and alleging bias.But both teams had requested an extension to voting times - Lula's had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as their reason.Both knew every vote would count and did not want their side to  miss out.The president of the Supreme Electoral Court Kássio Nunes Marques –  appointed by Jair Bolsonaro – confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voter extension did not change the outcome of the race.The sheer gap between the two candidates' tallies -  4.4 million votes - makes the result more difficult  to challenge.The result came as a surprise after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October with 47% of votes ahead of Lula's 45%.The right-wing candidate had been poised to give a victory speech and said the result should be annulled, calling it "inexplicable".But Lula's camp gained momentum ahead of election day, focusing on boosting voter turnout after 33 million people did not vote in round one. Sunday saw the largest drop in abstention between the two rounds of a presidential election since 1989.As disconsolate Bolsonaro supporters left the house in Brasília where their candidate had been watching the result, Lula took to the streets in São Paulo to celebrate and address his supporters."This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country," the former metal worker said. "It will be the one in which I listen most to the Brazilian people."Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin told him: "You, for the second time, have saved Brazilian democracy."Markets reacted negatively to the unexpected outcome. The Sao Paolo stock exchange opened 15% down, sparking a brief suspension before recovering slightly. Interest rate futures rose as investors scrutinised Lula's fiscal plans.Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has already been president for three non-consecutive terms, serving two terms between January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.His win makes him the first in Brazilian history to secure a fourth term, which will last until 2030.But this has been a bitterly fought campaign and the new term - set to start on 5 January - comes amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from the US president.Referring to what Trump has called the "Donroe Doctrine" -  which seeks to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere - Lula used his victory speech to insist that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard".Trump has previously shown support for Bolsonaro's father Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of a coup attempt after losing the 2022 elections to Lula. Flávio Bolsonaro met Trump at the White House earlier this year to bid for his support.Lula has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters in countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia have put right-wing candidates and parties in power.

schema.headline: Brazil election: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic comeback over Bolsonaro

title: ATP doubles proposals: Players and legends sign open letter to prevent cuts
description: Angry players urge ATP rethink over doubles cutsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Finland's Harri Heliovaara (left) and Britain's Henry Patten
body: Angry players urge ATP rethink over doubles cutsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Finland's Harri Heliovaara (left) and Britain's Henry Patten - the world number ones and reigning Wimbledon champions - have signed the open letterByBBC Sport tennis news reporterMore than 150 men's doubles players - including British world number one Henry Patten and the legendary Bryan brothers - have urged the ATP Tour to rethink "drastic" changes which they believe could kill the format.In a show of collective action, the players have written an open letter to the men's governing body as they fight proposals which would cut draw sizes and reduce prize money from 2028."We're at risk of losing a discipline of tennis which is historic - but has a big future," Dutch player Sem Verbeek, one of the architects of the letter, told BBC Sport."These proposals would destroy careers, livelihoods and dreams."The ATP proposed halving the doubles draws at its flagship Masters 1000 events to 16 teams, with smaller tournaments reduced to eight teams.The percentage of prize money devoted to doubles could fall from 20% to 10% - with the difference redistributed to singles players.On Monday, a group of 137 current players, 28 legends and 20 national federations signed a letter which they hope will pressure the ATP into rethinking the proposals.The tour's board - comprised of chairman Andrea Gaudenzi, four tournament representatives and four player representatives - will vote on the plans at next month's ATP Finals in Turin.The doubles reform is part of a wider review by the ATP, which it says is designed to "strengthen" the tour from 2028.The ATP aims to create "a more sustainable long-term model", insisting it wants to "maintain the important role" of doubles."Commercial success matters. Fairness, player welfare and the long-term health of tennis matter just as much," the players' letter says."Let us grow tennis together, without leaving doubles players behind."Why is doubles under threat?The proposals provoked an angry response from the men's doubles cohort when they were revealed in July.British pair Lloyd Glasspool and Julian Cash, who won Wimbledon in 2025 and became world number ones, accused the ATP of trying to "kill part of the sport".Others within tennis believe reform is needed. They suggest a 20% share of the prize money for doubles is disproportionate to the interest shown by fans.The doubles players argue the ATP should do more to promote their discipline and attract greater audiences, pointing out it is the format played by most club members and therefore more relatable.The ATP says the proposals are based on data-led analysis centred on costs, revenue and viewership.With fewer singles players now competing in doubles, it believes the current size of the standalone doubles events puts severe strain on tournaments."We support progress. We also understand the need to grow the sport, strengthen tournaments and increase commercial value," the players' letter says."Still, the proposed reforms go much too far."Might the dispute lead to legal action?Reigning Wimbledon champion Patten recently told BBC Sport the players were facing "an uphill battle", but remained "optimistic" the tour would consider counter-proposals. Since Wimbledon there have been several meetings between both sides, including recently at the Shanghai Masters.The players still believe there is little appetite for negotiation from the ATP. But ATP sources insist a compromise is likely to be found.Mike and Bob Bryan - the identical twins considered the greatest doubles pair of all-time - said they would support the group considering legal action to protect their discipline.In 2005, the American brothers led players in a lawsuit against the ATP, when it planned radical changes to doubles."The tour's in the healthiest financial state it's ever been - in our opinion it should be creating more opportunities," Bob Bryan told BBC Sport in an interview at Wimbledon in July.Mike Bryan added: "These proposed changes are anti-competitive. That's the stance we had to take in 2005. We still believe in doubles and we believe in the players fighting for this."

schema.headline: ATP doubles proposals: Players and legends sign open letter to prevent cuts

title: Bleach: Popular anime series officially ends as fans say goodbye
description: It's a finale fans have waited more than a decade to see.The epic conclusion to Bleach, the popular animated series based on the hit manga, or Japanes
body: It's a finale fans have waited more than a decade to see.The epic conclusion to Bleach, the popular animated series based on the hit manga, or Japanese comic, has arrived - and early reactions have described it is as a "perfect" ending. Anticipation for the final episode of the climactic Thousand-Year Blood War storyline was especially high.The original comic book's "rushed" ending is widely considered disappointing but creator Tite Kubo has overseen some major changes to the new adaptation. As some mourned the "end of an era", many waited nervously to see if he could stick the landing second time around.BBC Newsbeat's spoke to fans as they said an "emotional" goodbye to Kubo's creation. Bleach is regarded as one of the "big three" manga in Japan alongside One Piece and Naruto, and animated adaptations of each are credited with helping to fuel the global popularity of anime.It follows the story of Ichigo Kurosaki, a teenager with distinctive orange hair who has the unusual ability to see ghosts.He navigates school and family life at the same time as defending humanity from evil spirits. "It is honestly my favourite series of all time, it has got me through a lot across my life," says fan Ruby, 27.So how did it feel to say goodbye?"I honestly think I laughed more than I cried in this episode," she says."I'm just really happy that Kubo finally got to show us his true vision for the story that he wasn't able to back in the early 2010s." The 27-year-old started reading Bleach aged nine and became friends with fellow fan Nicholas, 30, through their shared passion."I've made so many friends through Bleach, it's been such a wonderful part of my life both in terms of what it teaches me and the kind of people I meet through it," says Ruby.For Nicholas, watching Bleach as teenager helped him get through school - and he even has a tattoo dedicated to the story."It helped me make friends in school, talking to a few people who also knew Bleach and about our favourite characters," he says.The pair tell Newsbeat they will be "crying together" as they watch the finale later."A lot of us are feeling quite emotional about it," says Ruby.Itanna Alakija describes himself as the "biggest Bleach fan there is" and says the revised finale was a "perfect conclusion to the entire arc of Bleach.The 28-year-old does think some people will be disappointed by the lack of action in the episode, but thinks the anime succeeded in taking the original manga "a step further".And a tease at the end of the episode has given Alakija hope that there might be more stories to come from the Bleach universe.Alakija says the series resonated with him because of its depiction of black characters, in contrast with other anime where creators can lean on stereotypes."The way that Tite Kubo integrates all these cultures and represents them in a Japanese art form is really interesting and amazing," the 28-year-old says.Alakija was already a Naruto fan when he discovered Bleach as a teenager."I remember stumbling upon Bleach and thought: 'This looks cool'," he says.And he praises the show for treating black characters as "normal people"."It's one of the few anime that has represented black characters in a non-stereotypical way."Bleach is available to stream via Disney+ globally and on Hulu in the US.

schema.headline: Bleach: Popular anime series officially ends as fans say goodbye

title: LIV Golf: Former US Open champion Graeme McDowell confirms exit
description: Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell has become the latest major champion to confirm his departure from LIV Golf. The 2010 US Open winner, McDowell, 47,
body: Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell has become the latest major champion to confirm his departure from LIV Golf. The 2010 US Open winner, McDowell, 47, announced on Monday he has "decided not to pursue" LIV 2.0, the new version of the breakaway tour which is due to start in 2027.Major winners Jon Rahm and Louis Oosthuizen have also confirmed their departures, while McDowell's fellow countryman Tom McKibbin said he was exiting LIV to return to the DP World Tour last week. England's Tyrrell Hatton and Ian Poulter have also left the competition. Saudi's Public Investment Fund withdrew its backing from LIV in April - having pumped in more than $5bn (£3.8bn) - leading to the league filing for bankruptcy protection in the United States last month.It has secured a possible $300m (£224m) in financing from BC Partners Credit to try to move forward with 'LIV 2.0', but only a handful of players have so far committed.Former world number four McDowell joined LIV when it launched as a lucrative Saudi Arabia-backed project in 2022.The 11-time DP World Tour winner's best finish on LIV was a tie for second in Virginia in June 2025."I've decided not to pursue LIV 2.0," said four-time Ryder Cup player McDowell. "I'm grateful for the opportunity I've had over the last four years and want to thank everyone who has been part of that journey."I look forward to the next chapter in my career."Earlier this year, McDowell told BBC Sport NI he had held "really positive" talks about returning to the DP World Tour next season, adding he was "lucky to have that option".

schema.headline: LIV Golf: Former US Open champion Graeme McDowell confirms exit

title: Women's Ballon d'Or 2026: Will anyone stop Alexia Putellas winning?
description: The reasons are obvious.In Barcelona, Spain boast the world's most dominant club side.The Catalans have contested seven of the past eight Champions Le
body: The reasons are obvious.In Barcelona, Spain boast the world's most dominant club side.The Catalans have contested seven of the past eight Champions League finals (winning four) and have been domestic champions every year since 2019-20, clinching the title by an average of 15 points above second place in that time.Then, there is the national team. World champions in 2023, losing finalists at the Euros to England in 2025 and then winners of the Nations League last December, beating Germany in the final.At the heart of all this success has been Putellas, who scored 21 goals and produced 13 assists during Barcelona's sensational season.And it is not just her output that makes her case. Her all-round influence captaining an already stellar side cannot be overstated. So, with 38 trophies in her possession already, the 2021 and 2022 Ballon d'Or winner appears poised to take it once again."Give it to her!" Spanish football expert Guillem Balague told BBC Sport. "Along with Marta, she is the best player in history. No doubt she was the best player in this campaign – and she won everything!"Unsurprisingly, Spain have more players on the shortlist than any other nation (six) and eight of the starting line-up from the Champions League final are in the running for this award.Among them are star striker Claudia Pina, who recently scored four against Real Madrid, goalkeeper Cata Coll and midfielder Patri Guijarro.While Putellas is now tormenting Women's Super League defences in the blue of London City, it is another forward in this country that perhaps has the best case for consideration.Khadija Shaw scored 21 goals in the league last season to fire Manchester City to their first title in a decade, adding another five in the FA Cup as they completed the double.The Jamaica striker has been the WSL's top scorer for the past three seasons, scored 90 goals since her arrival in summer 2021 and was rewarded with a lucrative four-year deal in June."We haven't had a major tournament but there are some amazing players on the list," said former England international Ellen White. "I would love to see Shaw up there - brilliant goalscoring."Shaw is part of a five-strong City contingent – they had none last season – but they all may fall short because they did not play in last season's Champions League.Arsenal's Alessia Russo was second to Shaw for goals last season and impressed in the Champions League, picking up nine goals.Last year, she came third in the Ballon d'Or voting last year behind Bonmati and club team-mate Mariona Caldentey.That came off the back of the Gunners' Champions League victory in May 2025. Exiting in the semi-finals to Lyon this year may cost her a shot at winning the award this year.One final candidate to break the Spanish stranglehold is, perhaps unsurprisingly, a Barcelona player. Poland's Ewa Pajor scored 11 goals in just 10 Champions League games last season, including a hat-trick in the final against Lyon.The 29-year-old won the Women's Gerd Muller trophy for top scorer last season and finished eighth in the overall rankings.Maybe it is her turn to take home the top prize.

schema.headline: Women's Ballon d'Or 2026: Will anyone stop Alexia Putellas winning?

title: England-Republic of Ireland Under-15 World Cup match abandoned over alleged racism
description: England walked off the pitch during a match at the Under-15 World Cup after an allegation of racism by a Republic of Ireland player, which resulted in
body: England walked off the pitch during a match at the Under-15 World Cup after an allegation of racism by a Republic of Ireland player, which resulted in the game being abandoned.Following an altercation between players from both sides, shortly before the end of the match in Azerbaijan on Monday, an England player approached his bench and made a complaint to coaching staff.Match footage then showed England staff members relaying the complaint to the referee, alleging a racist slur had been said, and calling their players off.Republic of Ireland were leading 4-1 at the time of the incident.World governing body Fifa told BBC Sport it is investigating and gathering reports."Fifa is aware of an incident at the U-15 World Cup and Festival match between England and the Republic of Ireland," a spokesperson said."The match was abandoned by the referee following England's refusal to continue."The official reports are being gathered, and the matter will be referred to the independent disciplinary committee, who will decide in due course."The Football Association and the Football Association of Ireland have been contacted for comment.The alleged incident happened in the final minute of the Group C match in Baku.Immediately following the allegation, England head coach Matt Thorpe was seen on the match coverage on DAZN asking for the referee to come over, before calling his players off the pitch.After an initial report from Thorpe, the referee told England's coaching staff, "I cannot hear".One of Thorpe's assistant coaches can then be heard telling the referee "we are reporting racism", before adding "we do not want to play".When another official came over, talking about what would happen after the match, the assistant told him: "No, our players do not want to play".He was later heard saying that a player was "upset".Heated words were then exchanged between each set of coaching staff, with both saying they were trying to protect their players.This is the first time the U15 World Cup and Festival has been played, and involves 189 countries and territories.Matches are played in an eight-a-side format, on smaller pitches, with 20-minute halves.England are scheduled to play their next match against Zimbabwe at 20:45 local time (16:45 GMT) on Monday, with Republic of Ireland facing Cambodia at the same time.

schema.headline: England-Republic of Ireland Under-15 World Cup match abandoned over alleged racism

title: Storm Boelo clean-up begins as thousands left without power
description: A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.The Energy
body: A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said around 22,600 properties are still without power as of Monday afternoon. Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old man in Dumfries and Galloway identified as Richard Baines, the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Garden.The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for strong winds from 18:00 on Monday to 03:00 on Tuesday across the west coast of England, Wales and Scotland and eastern parts of Northern Ireland.The Met Office has warned that further power cuts in areas covered by the warning are likely and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.Coastal communities could also be affected by spray or large waves, while travel delays are expected.Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England."Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," Slade told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.Marcus Reed, the operations director at a home fragrance manufacturer, said his factory and shop in Lyndal, Cumbria would be without power until Tuesday evening.He told the Today programme that he has had to turn away employees and customers."To lose two days manufacturing and distribution is going to be really disruptive," he said, adding that it was bad timing as it was "the busiest time of the year" for his business in the lead-up to Christmas."This is probably the worst situation I've experienced in my time here; we've had ad hoc issues over weekends where we've lost power, but it's been contained within a 12-hour period. It's the first time anything like this has happened, it's very serious."Wendy McKinney, whose bathroom shop in the seaside town of Largs in North Ayrshire was flooded on Sunday, told the Today programme the storm had been "devastating to local businesses".She said the local council only handed out sandbags after flooding had already started:"[They] were just left in the middle of the street yesterday afternoon on pallets just for everybody just to try and help themselves, but it was too little too late."North Ayrshire Council told the BBC that it had distributed almost 300 sandbags in Largs and Saltcoats and would continue to "respond where it has been safe and appropriate to do so".A spokesperson said council teams "followed established resilience procedures" but would review flooding reports and "consider any lessons that can be learned".

schema.headline: Storm Boelo clean-up begins as thousands left without power

title: Chris Brown: US singer given suspended eight-month prison sentence over nightclub attack
description: US singer Chris Brown has avoided jail after striking a man twice in the head with a glass tequila bottle in a London nightclub.The R&B star was given
body: US singer Chris Brown has avoided jail after striking a man twice in the head with a glass tequila bottle in a London nightclub.The R&B star was given an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, over the attack at private members' club Tape in Mayfair, in the early hours of 19 February 2023.Brown's vocal coach, rapper Omololu Akinlolu, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months. Both men, who had pleaded guilty to affray, were also ordered to pay £1,500 costs.Judge Tony Baumgartner said Brown's use of the glass bottle to hit the victim twice over the head "was plainly dangerous", adding that the violence of the attack was "intense".The sentence means Brown will not be imprisoned unless he commits another offence during the 12-month period of suspension. The court heard Brown's attack on music producer Abraham 'Abe' Diaw left the victim in need of hospital treatment for his injuries. In sentencing, Judge Baumgartner said: "The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained."CCTV footage was shown where Brown struck Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head, and then hitting his shoulder.Sentencing Brown, Judge Baumgartner said: "This was not planned violence. It was nevertheless serious violence by two people in a crowded nightclub."The judge told Brown: "Violence of this kind in a crowded nightclub is serious, it creates an obvious risk, not only to the person against whom it is directed, but also to others nearby."He added that Brown's conduct was "particularly dangerous" and that he had to be "physically pulled away" from the attack.The judge said Brown's fame, commercial success and professional standing "do not entitle you to special treatment - the law applies equally to everyone". But judge Baumgartner also said he had noted Brown's guilty plea, compliance with bail conditions, and the impact a custodial sentence would have on Brown's children, and said the singer's "risk of further offending is low".Brown and Akinlolu pleaded guilty to a charge of affray at Southwark Crown Court in July. The singer had been due to face a trial on more serious charges, which he denied, and which were subsequently dropped.These were assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and having an offensive weapon.Following Brown and Akinlolu's guilty pleas, the CPS released a statement outlining that Brown had approached Diaw on the dance floor, hitting him over the head with a glass bottle twice, before Akinlolu then punched Diaw in the head."They continued their assault whilst the victim attempted to flee through the club," the CPS said. "The victim was kicked while he was seated defenceless on the floor."Judge Baumgartner told the pair that while he had concluded they had both crossed the threshold to be jailed, this year's changes to sentencing laws meant that he had to put off doing so, unless there were exceptional reasons."I have considered whether the seriousness of the offending, taken together with the need for punishment and deterrence, amounts to exceptional circumstances requiring immediate imprisonment. I have concluded, in relation to each of you, that it does not," he said."These were serious offences deserving of custodial sentences, but the circumstances do not justify displacing the [new legal] requirement that those sentences be suspended."On Monday, the court was shown three pieces of CCTV footage from inside Tape nightclub on the night of the attack.The attack lasted no more than 20 seconds, but Brown could be seen hitting the victim four times with a tequila bottle, twice to the head.Prosecutor, Heidi Stonecliffe KC, described the weapon as a "heavy square-shaped tequila bottle" and said Diaw was approached by Brown at around 03:00.The footage showed that the nightclub was very small and packed at the time.The defence described Chris Brown as a "dedicated and a loving father of four children," someone who is "positive and present".The singer is described as having lived "a good and law-abiding life" since his last conviction in 2013.The events in Tape nightclub were described by the defence as a "short and deeply regretted incident".Brown's defence lawyer told the court that he apologises to all those present at the club at the time of the attack."This is an ugly and unattractive incident," Sallie Bennett-Jenkins KC said."It is, however, an incident which was very short-lived, lasting something more than 17 seconds but no more than 20."It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr Brown... offers a profound apology to all those present."The court heard Akinlolu "genuinely believed" that Brown was "under attack" when he joined the attack, punching Diaw.Brown was described as being like a "brother" to Akinlolu, his lawyer Laurie-Anne Power KC told the court.She added: "He genuinely believed him to be under attack and became involved, and thereafter accepts his initial involvement very quickly evolved into the events he has pleaded guilty to."Diaw was taken to St Mary's Hospital in London after the attack. Ms Stonecliffe KC said he was discharged with "pain relief and a diagnosis of head injury and superficial injury of the knee".An MRI scan taken in early March showed a "high grade injury to a ligament on the inner side of the left knee", the court heard.Defending Brown, Ms Bennett-Jenkins KC said there was a "relatively low level of force" and disputed how significant the injuries were.The defence argued that the attack left no fractures or broken skin and there was an absence of serious injuries.Diaw, the victim, was "not supportive of the prosecution" and "withdrew" his support some time after the incident, the court heard.Brown and Akinlolu stood up and faced one another and clasped hands after the judge concluded his sentencing remarks before walking out of the glass dock.There were loud cheers outside the court as Chris Brown left the building as he appeared to stop to sign an autograph.After the sentencing, Brown shared a video from inside his car on his Instagram story, showing him looking out the window before turning to the camera and giving a thumbs-up.Affray is an offence under the Public Order Act and a person is deemed guilty in law if they use or threaten "unlawful violence towards another" with their behaviour, leading someone to fear for their personal safety.Brown, 37, is considered one of the biggest stars in R&B, with a string of hit songs including Turn Up The Music, Ayo, Freaky Friday, Run It, Forever, Yeah 3x and Don't Wake Me Up.

schema.headline: Chris Brown: US singer given suspended eight-month prison sentence over nightclub attack

title: Bristol woman wins £127k High Court claim for mum's care at home
description: Daughter wins £127k claim for caring for mum at homeImage source, Family handoutImage caption, Bern says her mother wanted to be cared for at home by
body: Daughter wins £127k claim for caring for mum at homeImage source, Family handoutImage caption, Bern says her mother wanted to be cared for at home by her familyByMatty EdwardsBristol and Fiona LamdinWest of England home and social affairs correspondentA woman has described her "phenomenal" relief after she won a legal case that means she is entitled to be paid £127k from her mother's estate for caring for her in her final years.Bern Rogers, from Bristol, told the BBC of the "harrowing and deeply sad" family dispute since her elderly mother Sheila died in 2020, which led to her facing criminal charges.Legal experts said the "hugely significant" High Court ruling would lead to other claims.The executor of Sheila's estate, Bern's brother Andrew, said it had "always been willing to pay" her "genuine expenses" and an extra amount for her efforts. But the estate intends to appeal against the judgment that awarded Bern £127,500 for care provided.Bern looked after Sheila, who had dementia, for two-and-a-half years. After Sheila moved into Bern's house in Bristol in September 2017, she wanted to be cared for by her daughter rather than get costly home care or go into a residential care home.Crucially, Bern said she agreed with her mother she would be paid for the round-the-clock care.After Sheila died in April 2020, Bern took £100,000 from her estate. It led to her being reported to the police for fraud and theft. The money was seized and Bern was charged. But, at a trial at Bristol Crown Court in 2022, she was found not guilty by a jury.After being cleared, Bern turned to the civil courts. In 2025, a High Court judge ruled she had entered into an informal contract with Sheila for payment of a reasonable sum for her care.The estate was also ordered by a judge to pay Bern's legal costs.In August this year, another High Court judge worked out the amount Bern was due and ruled she was owed £127,500 for the 850 days of care she provided.Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Sheila was diagnosed with dementia after moving in with her daughter"Mum came to live with me, she became very confused and was seen wandering in the garden and obviously needed care," Bern said. "We didn't know what was wrong with her."She said caring for her mother had been like a full-time job, adding: "I couldn't leave her really. She became unpredictable."Sheila became more frail, was diagnosed with dementia and also had a series of physical health problems, including a "chronic" and "disabling" prolapse. Bern's husband Jon said: "It was relentless after she moved in with us. We couldn't go out even to the shops. It was a 24-hour job."It was a privilege, but we had to put our lives on hold for more than two years and revolve our lives around looking after her."He remembered that in Sheila's final weeks, his wife was sleeping on the floor of her mother's bedroom to make sure she was alright.'Devastating betrayal'Bern said "of course" she would have looked after her mother if she had not been able to pay her. But she said her mother had wanted to be looked after by her daughter rather than getting professional carers or going into a home, which would have cost thousands of pounds a month."She was very insistent and would tell anyone that would listen that she wanted to make sure that I sorted out money for her care, I was to make sure I got paid properly," she said.Multiple messages from Bern's five siblings were shown in court saying that she should be paid something for the care, although no amount was agreed.That is why, she explained, shortly after her mother had died, she transferred £100,000 from her mother's account. Bern was reported to the police for theft and fraud, which she describes as a "terrible and devastating betrayal"."It has been harrowing and deeply sad for it to go from a normal family relationship to being treated like a scapegoat, five against one," she said.Image caption, Bern Rogers says she and her husband Jon can get on with their lives now after the two High Court rulingsAfter the two separate High Court judgements in her favour, Bern said: "The weight off my shoulders was phenomenal."It has been absolutely wonderful to be vindicated. It means I can get on with my life now, the rest of my retirement."Jon said: "I'm very proud of her, actually, because she has stuck up for her mother, for carers and for herself."It's been a very long and tough journey of nine years, and we've finally got justice."'Future courts will follow'Legal experts have told the BBC that while this case does not automatically set a legal precedent, it is likely to lead to similar claims in future. Emma Holland, partner in trust and litigation at Stewarts, said: "What this case demonstrates is that the courts are willing to apply ordinary contractual principles to family relationships, which wasn't clear before."This means family members are more likely to be entitled to payment if there is an informal agreement, she said, even without an amount being agreed."These are considered, well-reasoned judgements by highly esteemed judges, so I would think it's very likely that future courts will follow them," Holland said.Beth Middleton, senior associate in private wealth and disputes at JMW, said this was a "hugely significant" case that would "open a floodgate of claims".Samara Dutton, partner at Collyer Bristow, who specialises in trusts, inheritance and wills, said the judgements were likely to be "influential". "It demonstrates a willingness to look beyond individual care tasks and acknowledges the broader reality of providing care to an elderly relative, including the continuous supervision, responsibility and restrictions on personal freedom," she said.Image caption, Bern Rogers and her husband Jon say they feel pride that their ordeal could help other family carers in futureBern said she was "terribly proud" that her case could influence others in future, which she said was her mum's "legacy"."It's a huge win for carers everywhere," Jon added, but stressed families still needed to have open discussions about what was fair.The ruling that states that Bern is entitled to payment cannot be appealed against, however, the estate intends to lodge an appeal against the second ruling that decided the amount owed. The executor of Sheila's estate is Bern's brother, Andrew Wills. In a statement on behalf of the estate, he said: "The only agreements that we (her siblings) were aware of was for my mother to give Bernadette £50 per week 'keep' and to ensure that Bernadette was not to be out of pocket.  "We were not made aware of any other contract between our mother and Bernadette."The statement added: "At all times I have attempted to be independent and to act in the best interests of the estate."The estate has always been willing to pay Bernadette her genuine expenses as well as an additional gratuity in recognition of her efforts for our mother."We have always tried to be fair. Unfortunately, our offers were not accepted by Bernadette who instead issued legal proceedings against the estate."Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Bristol woman wins £127k High Court claim for mum's care at home

title: John Healey's Budget to shield low-income pensioners from income tax
description: The chancellor's allies argue his plans for pensioners will mean they do not need to face an administrative burden just to pay a small amount of tax.M
body: The chancellor's allies argue his plans for pensioners will mean they do not need to face an administrative burden just to pay a small amount of tax.More specific details, including how many pensioners this will affect, have yet to be confirmed by the Treasury.The Budget is due to be printed this evening, with Healey's speech likely to be fine-tuned right up until it is delivered on Wednesday lunchtime.Treasury sources concede it will not involve the scale of tax and spending announcements seen from Labour and Conservative governments in recent years.The Tories are calling on the chancellor to cut green taxes, red tape and benefits to bring down energy bills.Reform is recommending the chancellor adopts 60 policies which they claim will create jobs - including approving the controversial Rosebank oil field - a project Healey is understood to back.Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper has called on the government to agree a new growth and defence partnership with the EU, including joining the single market. She argued this would help "ease the huge tax burden weighing people down".The Green Party has urged Healey to use his first Budget to "make the UK affordable", including by funding energy bill support by ending a tax relief for data centres.Senior Green politicians, including leader Zack Polanski, MPs and peers, made clear their suggestions in a letter to Healey.

schema.headline: John Healey's Budget to shield low-income pensioners from income tax

title: Backlash after Trump invokes 9/11 in attack on El-Sayed
description: US President Donald Trump is facing a backlash after invoking 9/11 as part of a verbal assault on Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for the US
body: US President Donald Trump is facing a backlash after invoking 9/11 as part of a verbal assault on Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Michigan.Speaking at a rally in the state on Sunday, Trump accused El-Sayed of being "a jihadist". He introduced as a guest speaker the father of a passenger who fought back against the 9/11 hijackers.Trump also suggested that El-Sayed would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate".Critics condemned Trump's attack as Islamophobic. El-Sayed himself responded to Trump's decision to refer to him by his middle name, Mohamed, saying during a rally of his own: "I'll be Senator Mohamed to you, bro."He also said: "They think that by pointing at my name and my faith, that somehow you're going to ignore the fact that you can't afford your gas or your groceries, can't see a doctor."Appearing alongside him, Senator Bernie Sanders said: "The reason they are using Islamophobia against Abdul is because they have nothing to say about the real issues."El-Sayed is taking on Republican candidate Mike Rogers on 3 November. The race is expected to be one of the closest in the midterm elections, and is proving to be particularly bitter.The seat is considered to be one of just a handful that could decide the balance of power in Congress. It is currently held by the Democrats.El-Sayed, a former public health official who was born in the US to Egyptian parents, will be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate if he wins the seat. He has previously dismissed the various attacks made against him by both Trump and Rogers and denied any connection to extremist groups.El-Sayed's opponents have sought to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist organisation that was founded in Egypt. Trump designated certain chapters of it as Foreign Terrorist Organisations earlier this year. Some of the scrutiny of the affiliations of El-Sayed and his family members relates to their writings from more than a decade ago. A social media post, external in 2012 by El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, appeared to refer to the movement, saying "my family has long been MB". El-Sayed's team have previously distanced him from other comments by Abdelhadi.Critics have also pointed to an opinion piece El-Sayed wrote in Huffington Post in 2011, external about pro-democracy protesters in Egypt. In it, he acknowledged concerns that "supporting democracy in Egypt might allow the country to fall to the hands of the Muslim Brotherhood".A year later he also allegedly signed an open letter by Egyptian Americans. In it, the group urged Mohamed Morsi, Egypt's first democratically elected president and a leader of the Muslim Brotherhood, to "purge the media and police" following the toppling of the authoritarian regime in the Arab Spring. This letter has not been discussed by El-Sayed.El-Sayed has previously denied any connection to the Muslim Brotherhood and has stressed his loyalty to the United States. Asked recently at a town hall event whether he would disavow the organisation, he responded: "Absolutely."Also in 2012, El-Sayed's current opponent Rogers, who was then a US representative and chairing the House Intelligence Committee, appeared to call for cautious engagement with the Muslim Brotherhood, telling Reuters, external: "Do I think there are moderate Muslim Brotherhood individuals we are going to have to reach out to and talk to? Yes but we are going to have to watch it carefully."

schema.headline: Backlash after Trump invokes 9/11 in attack on El-Sayed

title: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak
description: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in South
body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December by Vickrum Digwa, who falsely claimed he had been racially abused and had acted in self-defence. Digwa was jailed for life on 1 June, with a minimum term of 21 years.Following the teenager's murder, police bodycam footage of him being handcuffed as he lay dying led to intense scrutiny of the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary and sparked wider debates around knife laws, race, policing and public trust. The review, which was welcomed by Nowak's family, will be led by former Justice Secretary Alex Chalk KC."We must get to truth of what happened before, during and after that awful night and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate," Mahmood told the House of Commons on Monday. Mahmood said the review will investigate what was known about Nowak's killer and if there were missed opportunities to intervene as well as the treatment of his family in the justice system and whether they received enough support.In a statement published on Monday, the Home Office said the review will be carried out in two parts.Phase one will cover the police, health services, local authorities educational institutions and faith organisations, including if any concerns were raised relating to weapon possession and violent behavior, the statement said. It will also look to determine if there were missed opportunities to prevent Nowak's murder. Phase two will follow after the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has concluded its investigation into the actions of police officers who attended the scene. It will consider the actions of the IOPC and "if necessary" the police, the Home Office added. The IOPC launched its own investigation into the response on the night of Nowak's death after bodycam footage showed the 18-year-old was handcuffed and left dying on the floor despite informing officers of his injuries.The investigation was launched despite a sentencing judge ruling Nowak would not have survived his injuries, however quickly he received treatment.The Nowak family described the announcement as a "significant moment in our fight for justice.""We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for," they added in a statement."Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have." Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed the decision to launch the review."There must be proper accountability for those who failed Henry and his family," she said.The review is due to report in five months. Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was a first-year accountancy and finance student at the University of Southampton when he was murdered.On the night of Nowak's muder, it was Digwa's brother who called 999, claiming Vickrum had been attacked "racially".Bodycam footage released by Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary, with the permission of Nowak's family, showed officers speaking to Digwa and others while Nowak lay on the ground.Nowak could be heard repeatedly saying that he had been stabbed and could not breathe.Violent disorder broke out in Southampton in the days following the release of the footage.After Digwa's sentencing, Nowak's father Mark called for a "full, fearless and transparent" investigation into the police response.But he also urged people not to use his son's death to "create further division, hatred or tension".

schema.headline: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak
